subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Ancient Tea Trees of Yunnan
description: A micro-lesson that makes Ancient Tea Trees of Yunnan usable.

hook.text: Yunnan has wild tea trees over 1,000 years old. They're taller than houses and treated as national treasures.

buildup.text: Ancient tree (gushu) tea has deep roots that access minerals and water younger plants can't reach.

discovery.text: Gushu pu-erh has more complex, layered flavor—mineral depth and a lingering sweetness called 'huigan.'

twist.text: Demand for gushu tea has made some villagers wealthy, but over-picking threatens the ancient trees' survival.

climax.text: Conservation efforts now limit harvesting on the oldest trees. Sustainability battles short-term profit.

punchline.text: Trees older than empires, making tea that money can't replicate.

quiz.question: What is 'gushu' tea?
options: Tea from ancient trees with deep roots and complex flavor

details.summary: Yunnan province is home to wild and cultivated tea trees that are hundreds and sometimes over a thousand years old. These ancient trees, called gushu, produce leaves with exceptional depth, complexity, and a distinctive huigan, or returning sweetness. Gushu pu-erh commands extreme premium prices.
details.whyItMatters: Ancient tea trees connect modern tea culture to millennia of history. Their survival in Yunnan's forests provides genetic diversity crucial for future tea breeding.
takeaways: Some tea trees in Yunnan are over 1,000 years old
Gushu trees produce tea with exceptional depth and sweetness
Ancient tree pu-erh commands the highest prices in the market

faq.question: How are ancient tea trees different from plantation tea?
faq.answer: Ancient trees have deep root systems that access minerals ordinary bushes cannot reach. They grow slowly, concentrating flavor compounds. Their leaves are larger, thicker, and more complex. The resulting tea has more body, sweetness, and a persistent aftertaste that plantation tea cannot match.

faq.question: Are ancient tea trees threatened?
faq.answer: Yes. High demand has led to over-picking, aggressive pruning, and even poisoning of surrounding trees to eliminate competition. Some villages have imposed harvest restrictions. Climate change and development also threaten forest habitats. Conservation efforts are growing but face economic pressure.
